name: Plant sterols and stanols
short: Raise blood plant-sterol levels and lower beta-carotene; a 2023 review says genetic studies raise unresolved heart-disease concerns. Trial meta-analysis: pooled withdrawal rate for adverse effects 0%.
text: In a 2005 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (its title concerns hyperlipidemia, or raised blood lipids; the abstract does not describe the participants further), the analysis of LDL cholesterol included 893 patients given plant sterol and stanol esters and 769 given placebo in 23 studies; across 20 studies, the pooled rate of withdrawal because of adverse effects with plant sterols and stanols was 0%, and the combined relative risk of withdrawal was 0.84 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.95, p = 0.69, not significant). The abstract does not say which adverse effects, if any, occurred. A 2003 expert review, drawing on meta-analyses of 10 to 15 trials per vitamin, reports that blood levels of vitamins A and D were not affected and alpha-carotene, lycopene and vitamin E stayed stable relative to LDL, but beta-carotene levels declined, although the experts did not expect adverse health outcomes from this; sterol-enriched foods also increased blood plant-sterol levels, and the experts discussed whether this could raise heart-disease risk, given the marked atherosclerosis seen in people with the inherited condition homozygous phytosterolemia, judging that risk largely hypothetical; the same review states that there are insufficient data to say whether plant stanols or sterols prevent or promote colon cancer, and that population follow-up has limited power to detect infrequent increases in common diseases. A 2023 review notes that there are no randomized trials of long-term safety or of cardiovascular events, that observational studies of plant sterols and heart disease have given conflicting results, and that recent genetic studies linking higher blood plant-sterol levels with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease have raised concerns about the safety of supplementation; these are associations, not shown effects of supplements. The cited abstracts describe no harmful interaction with medicines.
